city.name: Milan
city.elevationNote: Central Milan is almost completely flat, so the climbs mode is unavailable for this city.

source.note: Hand-written seed data for the demo. Coordinates are approximate (within roughly 50 m) and should be checked or replaced by running scripts/pipeline. Text sticks to well-documented facts; no quotations are used.

places.name: Milan Cathedral (Duomo)
places.summary: Construction of the cathedral began in 1386 and continued for almost six centuries. It is one of the largest churches in the world and a defining example of Italian Gothic architecture.
places.then: Work started under Archbishop Antonio da Saluzzo and Gian Galeazzo Visconti, on the site of older churches. The façade was only finished in the early 19th century at Napoleon's order.
places.now: The gilded Madonnina statue tops the highest spire, and visitors can walk among the pinnacles on the roof terraces.
places.more: Marble for the cathedral was quarried at Candoglia near Lake Maggiore and carried to Milan along the Naviglio canals. The building's forest of spires and statues was added slowly over the centuries, which is why its style mixes Gothic with later Renaissance, Baroque and neo-Gothic details. The Veneranda Fabbrica, the body founded to build the cathedral, still looks after it today.

places.name: Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
places.summary: A glass-and-iron covered arcade linking Piazza del Duomo and Piazza della Scala, designed by Giuseppe Mengoni. It is one of the oldest shopping galleries in the world.
places.then: It was built shortly after Italian unification and named after the first king of Italy. Mengoni died in a fall from the scaffolding shortly before the gallery was completed.
places.now: It still hosts cafés and luxury shops. Visitors spin on the heel over the mosaic bull in the floor for good luck.
places.more: The arcade is shaped like a Latin cross with a large glass dome over the central octagon. The floor mosaics show the coats of arms of the capitals of the newly unified kingdom: Milan, Turin, Florence and Rome. The bull represents Turin.

places.name: Teatro alla Scala
places.summary: One of the most famous opera houses in the world, designed by Giuseppe Piermarini and opened in 1778. Many operas by Verdi, Puccini and others had their premieres here.
places.then: It takes its name from the church of Santa Maria alla Scala, which was demolished to make room for it.
places.now: The theatre was bombed in 1943 and rebuilt; it reopened in 1946 with a concert conducted by Arturo Toscanini. Its season traditionally opens on 7 December, the feast of Milan's patron saint Ambrose.
places.more: The relatively plain façade hides a horseshoe-shaped auditorium with tiers of boxes. The adjoining Museo Teatrale holds costumes, instruments and portraits from the theatre's history.

places.name: Palazzo Reale
places.summary: For centuries this palace beside the cathedral was the seat of Milan's government. Its current neoclassical look comes from Giuseppe Piermarini's remodelling for the Habsburgs in the 1770s.
places.then: It housed Milan's rulers from the medieval communal period through the Viscontis, the Spanish, the Austrians and Napoleon.
places.now: The palace was badly damaged by bombing in 1943. It is now one of the city's main exhibition venues.
places.more: The Sala delle Cariatidi, the great ballroom, was deliberately left with its wartime damage as a memorial. In 1953 it hosted a famous exhibition of Picasso's Guernica.

places.name: Castello Sforzesco
places.summary: Francesco Sforza began rebuilding this fortress in the 1450s on the remains of a Visconti castle. It became the court of the Sforza dukes, where Leonardo da Vinci worked for Ludovico il Moro.
places.then: Under the Sforza it was one of the most splendid Renaissance courts in Italy. Later it served as a military barracks under Spanish and Austrian rule.
places.now: Architect Luca Beltrami restored it at the end of the 19th century. Today it houses several civic museums, including Michelangelo's last sculpture, the Rondanini Pietà.
places.more: Inside, the Sala delle Asse has a ceiling of intertwined tree branches painted by Leonardo. The Filarete Tower over the main gate is a reconstruction of the original, which was destroyed in an explosion in the 16th century. Behind the castle stretches Parco Sempione, which was once the dukes' hunting grounds.

places.name: Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio
places.summary: Founded by Bishop Ambrose in the late 4th century, when Milan was an imperial capital. The present building is a model of Lombard Romanesque architecture from the 11th and 12th centuries.
places.then: Ambrose was one of the most influential bishops of late antiquity and is now Milan's patron saint. He is buried in the crypt.
places.now: The arcaded atrium in front of the church is one of the best-preserved Romanesque spaces in Italy and is open to passers-by.
places.more: The two bell towers are from different centuries and tell the story of a rivalry between the monks and the canons who shared the basilica. Inside, the golden altar is a masterpiece of Carolingian metalwork from the 9th century.

places.name: Santa Maria delle Grazie
places.summary: A convent church whose refectory holds Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, painted around 1495–1498. Together with the church it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.then: Ludovico il Moro intended the church as a Sforza family mausoleum and had its east end rebuilt with a domed tribune often attributed to Bramante.
places.now: The refectory was hit by bombs in 1943, but the wall with the Last Supper had been protected with sandbags and survived. Visits are by timed reservation.
places.more: Leonardo painted the Last Supper on a dry wall instead of using true fresco, so it began to deteriorate within his lifetime. A long restoration ended in 1999. On the opposite wall is a Crucifixion by Donato da Montorfano.

places.name: Columns of San Lorenzo
places.summary: A row of sixteen Roman marble columns taken from an earlier building and set up in front of the basilica of San Lorenzo in late antiquity. They are among the most visible remains of Roman Mediolanum.
places.then: Mediolanum was a capital of the Western Roman Empire from the late 3rd century, and buildings from that era were reused when the basilica was built.
places.now: The square between the columns and the church is one of Milan's favourite evening meeting spots. A bronze copy of a statue of Emperor Constantine stands in front.
places.more: The columns once stood on the edge of the Roman city. The tram line runs just behind them along Corso di Porta Ticinese.

places.name: Basilica of San Lorenzo Maggiore
places.summary: One of the oldest churches in Milan, built in late antiquity as a vast centrally planned building. Its dome was rebuilt in the late 16th century.
places.then: It was built when Milan was an imperial residence, possibly as a court church.
places.now: The Chapel of Sant'Aquilino still preserves early Christian mosaics from the 4th century.
places.more: Below the Chapel of Sant'Aquilino you can see large blocks of reused Roman stone in the foundations. The church has burned and been rebuilt several times, but it kept its original four-lobed plan.

places.name: Pinacoteca di Brera
places.summary: A major picture gallery in Palazzo Brera, a 17th-century former Jesuit college designed by Francesco Maria Richini. The gallery opened in 1809 under Napoleonic rule.
places.then: Many of its paintings came from churches and monasteries closed in the Napoleonic period.
places.now: The palace also houses the Academy of Fine Arts, a library and an astronomical observatory. Its courtyard features a bronze statue of Napoleon after Canova.
places.more: Highlights include Mantegna's Lamentation of Christ, Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin and Hayez's The Kiss. The surrounding Brera district, with its narrow streets, was historically the artists' quarter.

places.name: San Maurizio al Monastero Maggiore
places.summary: A plain façade on Corso Magenta hides an interior completely covered in 16th-century frescoes, largely by Bernardino Luini and his workshop. It is often called the Sistine Chapel of Milan.
places.then: The church belonged to the Monastero Maggiore, the most important Benedictine convent in the city. A wall split the space between the public and the cloistered nuns.
places.now: Entry is free. The church is also used for concerts thanks to its historic organ.
places.more: The nuns' hall behind the dividing wall is just as richly painted as the public side. Next door, in the former monastery, is Milan's Archaeological Museum.

places.name: Roman Tower of the Maximian Walls
places.summary: A polygonal tower from the city walls built when Emperor Maximian made Mediolanum his capital at the end of the 3rd century. It survives in the courtyard of the Archaeological Museum.
places.then: The walls enclosed the imperial city, which for about a century was one of the capitals of the Western Roman Empire.
places.now: Medieval frescoes survive on the inside of the tower. Part of the Roman circus wall stands nearby.
places.more: The museum covers Roman, Etruscan and Greek collections, as well as early medieval Lombard finds. Milan's Roman layout can still be traced in the curve of some city-centre streets.

places.name: Arco della Pace
places.summary: A neoclassical triumphal arch by Luigi Cagnola, begun in 1807 to celebrate Napoleon. It was completed in 1838 under Austrian rule and dedicated to peace.
places.then: The arch marks the start of the road to Paris through the Simplon Pass, which Napoleon had built.
places.now: It closes the far end of Parco Sempione, opposite Castello Sforzesco, and the area around it is popular for evening drinks.
places.more: The bronze chariot of peace on top is pulled by six horses. When Napoleon III and Victor Emmanuel II entered Milan in 1859, the arch became a symbol of the Italian independence movement.

places.name: Biblioteca Ambrosiana
places.summary: One of the first public libraries in Europe, founded by Cardinal Federico Borromeo and opened in 1609. Its picture gallery was added soon after.
places.then: Borromeo built it as a centre of learning in the spirit of the Catholic Reformation.
places.now: It holds Leonardo's Codex Atlanticus, Caravaggio's Basket of Fruit and Raphael's full-size cartoon for The School of Athens.
places.more: The Codex Atlanticus is the largest collection of Leonardo's drawings and notes, with designs for machines, weapons and architecture. Pages are shown in rotating exhibitions.

places.name: Palazzo della Ragione
places.summary: The medieval town hall of Milan, built in the 13th century in Piazza dei Mercanti. Its open arcades at ground level once served as a market.
places.then: Piazza dei Mercanti was the political and commercial heart of the medieval free commune. A relief on the façade shows the podestà Oldrado da Tresseno on horseback.
places.now: Today the hall upstairs is used for photography exhibitions, and the square is a quiet shortcut just steps from the Duomo.
places.more: An extra floor was added to the building in the 18th century, which is why you can see two styles of windows. The neighbouring Loggia dei Mercanti dates from the early 14th century.

places.name: Santa Maria presso San Satiro
places.summary: A small church famous for Bramante's illusionistic choir. With no space to build a real apse, he painted and modelled a perspective that looks deep but is actually very shallow.
places.then: Bramante worked in Milan at the Sforza court before moving to Rome, where he designed the new St Peter's Basilica.
places.now: Walk toward the altar and step to the side to see the illusion break down.
places.more: Next to the church is the Sacello di San Satiro, a chapel founded in the 9th century and one of the oldest surviving buildings in the city centre.

places.name: Ca' Granda (Ospedale Maggiore)
places.summary: A great hospital founded by Francesco Sforza in 1456 and designed by Filarete. It brought together many smaller hospitals and served the city for centuries.
places.then: Its plan with courtyards and separate wards was considered very advanced for its time.
places.now: After heavy bomb damage in 1943 it was restored, and it now houses the University of Milan. Its courtyards are open to visitors.
places.more: The façade along Via Festa del Perdono mixes Filarete's Renaissance terracotta windows with later additions. The name Ca' Granda means 'big house' in the Milanese dialect.

places.name: San Bernardino alle Ossa
places.summary: A small church with an ossuary chapel whose walls are decorated with human skulls and bones. The bones came from nearby cemeteries and the hospital.
places.then: The chapel was rebuilt in the 17th century, and its vault was frescoed by Sebastiano Ricci.
places.now: It's a short detour from the Duomo and one of the city's most surprising interiors.
places.more: The contrast between the bright painted vault, which shows a triumph of souls among angels, and the bone-covered walls is deliberate: it is a reminder of death and resurrection.

places.name: Torre Velasca
places.summary: A skyscraper by the BBPR architects, completed in 1958. Its top floors jut out like a mushroom, in a deliberate echo of medieval Lombard castle towers.
places.then: It was built during the post-war reconstruction and sparked debate about modern architecture in historic city centres.
places.now: It remains one of Milan's most recognisable and divisive buildings, standing about 100 metres tall.
places.more: The wider upper section held apartments and the narrower lower part held offices. The shape grew from that mix of uses as well as the nod to history.

places.name: Palazzo Marino
places.summary: A palace designed by Galeazzo Alessi for the Genoese banker Tommaso Marino, begun in 1557. It has been Milan's city hall since 1861.
places.then: Marino was one of the richest men of his time, and the palace was intended to display that wealth.
places.now: The main façade facing Piazza della Scala is a 19th-century addition. The richly decorated courtyard is the original.
places.more: The Sala Alessi, the grand hall, is used for city ceremonies and is occasionally open to the public.

places.name: Casa degli Omenoni
places.summary: The house of the sculptor Leone Leoni, whose façade is held up by eight giant stone figures. Milanese people call them 'omenoni', meaning big men.
places.then: Leoni was court sculptor to Emperor Charles V and decorated his own house to advertise his skill.
places.now: It's a private building on a quiet side street just behind Piazza della Scala, so most people walk past without noticing.
places.more: The figures are telamons, the male equivalent of caryatids, and are thought to represent barbarians defeated by Rome.

places.name: San Gottardo in Corte
places.summary: The former court chapel of Azzone Visconti, tucked behind Palazzo Reale. Its octagonal brick bell tower is a fine example of Lombard Gothic.
places.then: The bell tower is known for one of the earliest public striking clocks in Italy, installed in the 14th century.
places.now: Most visitors to the Duomo never see it, though it is only a couple of minutes' walk away.
places.more: Inside is the tomb of Azzone Visconti, lord of Milan, who greatly enlarged the city's court and public buildings.

places.name: San Fedele
places.summary: A Jesuit church begun in 1569 to a design by Pellegrino Tibaldi, commissioned by Archbishop Carlo Borromeo. It became a model for Counter-Reformation churches in Lombardy.
places.then: The writer Alessandro Manzoni attended this church. In 1873 he fell on its steps and died a few months later.
places.now: A statue of Manzoni stands in the middle of Piazza San Fedele.
places.more: Inside, the single wide nave was designed so that the congregation could see and hear the preacher clearly, in line with the reforms of the Council of Trent.

places.name: Casa del Manzoni
places.summary: The house where Alessandro Manzoni, author of The Betrothed, lived from 1814 until his death in 1873. It is now a museum and study centre.
places.then: Visitors here included Giuseppe Verdi and Giuseppe Garibaldi. Verdi later composed his Requiem in Manzoni's memory.
places.now: His study is preserved much as he left it, and the house holds manuscripts and early editions.
places.more: The Betrothed, set in 17th-century Lombardy, became a founding text of modern Italian literature. Manzoni revised its language using Florentine Italian.

places.name: Museo Poldi Pezzoli
places.summary: The home and collection of the nobleman Gian Giacomo Poldi Pezzoli, opened as a museum in 1881. It is one of Europe's finest house museums.
places.then: He arranged his rooms in historical styles to match the art he collected.
places.now: Its best-known work is the Portrait of a Young Woman attributed to Piero del Pollaiolo, which has become the museum's emblem.
places.more: The collection also includes arms and armour, clocks, textiles, and paintings by Botticelli and Mantegna.

places.name: Basilica of Sant'Eustorgio
places.summary: A historic basilica linked to the tradition of the relics of the Three Magi. Its Portinari Chapel is an early Renaissance jewel with frescoes by Vincenzo Foppa.
places.then: In 1164, after Frederick Barbarossa's conquest of Milan, the relics were taken to Cologne. A small part was returned in 1903.
places.now: The Feast of the Epiphany is still celebrated here with a procession of the Magi from the Duomo.
places.more: The Portinari Chapel was commissioned by Pigello Portinari, who managed the Medici bank in Milan. Its frescoes show the life of Saint Peter Martyr, whose tomb stands in the centre.

places.name: Archi di Porta Nuova
places.summary: A medieval city gate from the walls rebuilt after Milan was destroyed by Frederick Barbarossa's forces in 1162. Roman gravestones were reused in its masonry.
places.then: The gate was the northern entrance to the medieval city on the road toward Como.
places.now: Today traffic flows through its twin arches, and the Roman inscriptions can be spotted in the stonework.
places.more: The tabernacle with statues of the Madonna and saints on the outer face was added in the 14th century.

places.name: Darsena and Naviglio Grande
places.summary: Milan's old inland harbour, where the Naviglio Grande canal met the city. The Naviglio Grande is one of the oldest navigable canals in Europe.
places.then: Boats brought marble for the cathedral, along with grain, timber and goods, into the city along this canal network.
places.now: The basin was restored and reopened in 2015, and its banks are now a busy promenade lined with bars.
places.more: Leonardo da Vinci studied the Milanese canals and their locks. Most of the inner canal ring was covered over in the 1920s and 1930s.

places.name: Vicolo dei Lavandai
places.summary: A narrow alley off the Naviglio Grande where washerwomen once scrubbed laundry in a small channel under a wooden roof. The stone washboards are still in place.
places.then: Washing clothes in the canal water was hard work and a common job for working-class families along the Navigli.
places.now: It is one of the most photographed corners of the Navigli district.
places.more: Despite the name, the washers here were mostly women. The canal side was once full of workshops, mills and laundries.

places.name: Basilica of San Simpliciano
places.summary: One of the basilicas founded by Saint Ambrose and completed by his successor Simplicianus. Much of its late antique brick structure survives under later alterations.
places.then: According to tradition, three doves flew from the martyrs' relics here to the battlefield of Legnano in 1176, where the Lombard League defeated Barbarossa.
places.now: It's a calm stop in the Brera district, with a fresco of the Coronation of the Virgin by Bergognone in the apse.
places.more: Ambrose founded several basilicas around Milan, one for each category of saints. This one was known as the Basilica of the Virgins.

places.name: San Nazaro in Brolo
places.summary: Founded by Saint Ambrose as the Basilica of the Apostles in the late 4th century. In front stands the Trivulzio Chapel, designed by Bramantino in the early 16th century.
places.then: The church stood beside the road leading out of Roman Milan toward Rome.
places.now: The bold geometric Trivulzio Chapel, the burial place of the condottiero Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, now serves as the church's entrance.
places.more: The cross-shaped plan of the early church is one of the first of its kind in the West.

places.name: Leonardo's Vineyard (Casa degli Atellani)
places.summary: Ludovico il Moro gave Leonardo da Vinci a vineyard here while he was painting the Last Supper across the street. The vineyard was replanted and opened to visitors in 2015.
places.then: The Casa degli Atellani was a residence of courtiers of the Sforza family.
places.now: The house and garden can be visited with a ticket, just opposite Santa Maria delle Grazie.
places.more: Researchers used genetic analysis of surviving roots to identify the grape variety Leonardo grew before the vines were replanted.

places.name: Palazzo Mezzanotte (Stock Exchange)
places.summary: The Milan Stock Exchange building, designed by Paolo Mezzanotte and completed in 1932. The remains of a Roman theatre were found under its foundations.
places.then: Mediolanum's Roman theatre stood here, and traces of it can be seen in the basement.
places.now: In front stands Maurizio Cattelan's marble sculpture L.O.V.E. from 2010, a hand with only the middle finger raised, pointing at the stock exchange.
places.more: Piazza degli Affari is a showcase of the monumental architecture of the 1930s.

places.name: San Marco
places.summary: A large Augustinian church founded in the 13th century in the Brera district. It is linked to two famous composers.
places.then: The young Mozart stayed in the adjoining convent in 1770.
places.now: Verdi's Requiem had its premiere here in 1874, a year after Manzoni's death.
places.more: The church faced a small harbour on the covered-over Naviglio canal, whose route is now marked by Via San Marco.

places.name: Conca dell'Incoronata
places.summary: A surviving lock of the Naviglio della Martesana canal, hidden on a quiet street. It is often linked to the lock designs Leonardo da Vinci studied in Milan.
places.then: Locks like this one let boats climb and descend between different water levels on their way into the city.
places.now: The canal here was filled in, but the stone basin and wooden gates still survive as a reminder of the vanished waterways.
places.more: Leonardo's notebooks contain drawings of mitre gates, the angled lock gates still used on canals around the world.

places.name: Palazzo Litta
places.summary: A grand aristocratic palace on Corso Magenta, begun in the 1640s. Its long rococo façade was added in the 18th century.
places.then: The Litta family were among the most powerful nobles of Milan.
places.now: The palace houses public offices and a theatre, and its staircase and halls open for special events.
places.more: The Teatro Litta in the palace complex is one of the oldest theatres in Milan still in use.

places.name: Palazzo Clerici
places.summary: A noble palace on a narrow street near La Scala, famous for a huge ceiling fresco painted by Giambattista Tiepolo in 1740.
places.then: The fresco shows the chariot of the sun crossing a sky full of mythological figures, and was meant to glorify the Clerici family.
places.now: The palace is home to a foreign policy institute and opens its gallery only on special occasions.
places.more: The fresco is one of Tiepolo's major works outside Venice.

places.name: Remains of the Imperial Palace (Via Brisa)
places.summary: Ruins of part of the imperial palace of Mediolanum, exposed when Second World War bombing cleared the area.
places.then: The palace complex was the residence of emperors when Milan was a capital of the Western Empire.
places.now: The ruins sit in an open pit in the middle of a quiet street, visible from the railings.
places.more: Milan hosted the meeting that led to the Edict of Milan in 313, which granted religious tolerance to Christians across the empire.

places.name: Villa Necchi Campiglio
places.summary: A 1930s villa by architect Piero Portaluppi, built for a wealthy industrial family. It had one of the first private swimming pools in Milan.
places.then: It reflects the lifestyle of the Milanese upper class between the wars.
places.now: It is run by FAI, the Italian national trust, and was a filming location for the movie I Am Love.
places.more: Inside you'll find early home technology and Art Deco furnishings, plus art collections donated to the house.
